title: Which caching policy is that?

prereqs.why: Each pairing is a policy and the behaviour — good and bad — that follows from it.
These are the same policies a CPU cache implements, in a different setting and at a different scale.

statement:
Five caching policies, and what each one actually does. Pair them up.

Note that two separate decisions are mixed in here: **where a write goes**, and **who is responsible for filling a miss**. Keeping those apart is most of the work.

One description on the right is not a caching policy at all.
hints: Three of these are about writes and two are about reads. Sorting them into those groups first halves the problem.
Of the write policies, one is the safest, one is the fastest, and one skips the cache altogether. The trade is between staleness, latency and what happens if the cache dies.
Of the read policies, the difference is whether the *application* or the *cache* knows how to reach the underlying store.

right: On a read miss the application fetches from the store and populates the cache itself; the cache knows nothing about the store
Every write goes to the cache and the store together, so the cache is never stale and writes pay the slow path every time
Writes land in the cache and are flushed to the store later, which is the fastest option and loses data if the cache dies before the flush
Writes bypass the cache entirely and go straight to the store, which suits data that is written once and rarely read back
On a read miss the cache itself fetches from the store and fills the entry, so the application only ever talks to the cache
Two caches keep a value consistent by broadcasting an invalidation to each other on every write
